text:
A: Alright? Can you hear me okay? I'm Gary.
B: Yeah. Alright. Callum.
A: Callum, lovely. Last one of these for me, I think. Where are you based then?
B: Swindon.
A: Swindon! I'm Bridgwater, down the M5. My uncle used to drive up to Swindon for the Honda plant, delivering parts, years ago.
B: My dad worked at Honda. Till it shut.
A: Did he? Oh, that was a shame, that, all them jobs. Is he alright now?
B: Yeah, he's alright. Found something else in the end.
A: Good, good. And what about you, are you working, mate?
B: Not at the minute. Took redundancy from a sports shop, I was assistant manager. Looking at warehouse stuff now.
A: Warehouse! Well, you've come to the right bloke. Nineteen years I was at a food depot, forklift, goods in, all that. Till my back packed in. Prolapsed disc, sciatica down the leg. I'm fifty-six going on ninety. And do you know, the lad I just spoke to, Daniel, he runs a big distribution centre, he was telling me about gatehouse jobs. Checking the drivers in, the paperwork, you're sat down most of the day. I'd never even thought of it.
B: Yeah, I spoke to him first. He said I should change my CV. Make it less retail.
A: Have you done it?
B: Erm. No.
A: Ha! Honest, I like that. I'm the same with the crossword, I'll leave the hard one and tell myself I'll come back to it. Have you got a forklift licence?
B: No. Never done one.
A: Worth asking the job centre. They can sometimes sort you a course, counterbalance, a few days. Once you've got that card, the agencies love you. I've still got mine in my wallet, lapsed mind, but I keep it. Daft really.
B: I didn't know they did that.
A: Oh yeah, ask your work coach. Tell him Gary from Bridgwater sent you. He won't know who I am, mind. Anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one.
B: Nah, it's alright. That's useful actually.
A: Who do you support, then, Swindon?
B: Yeah. They're rubbish though.
A: I'm Bristol City, so I can't talk. Family thing, my dad took me. Mostly I just watch the highlights now.
B: Same. Just check the score on my phone.
A: Do you get out much? Five-a-side or anything?
B: Used to. Not now. Mostly PlayStation, to be honest.
A: My granddaughter's four and she beats me at that Mario thing at my daughter's. Calls me Grumpa when I lose.
B: Ha. Grumpa.
A: Cheeky madam. Have you got a partner, kids?
B: Girlfriend, Jess. She's a dental nurse. No kids.
A: Six months, a year?
B: Six years.
A: Six years! She's a keeper then. Is she alright with you being off?
B: Yeah. Sort of. She's paying most of the bills at the minute. Which, yeah. Not great.
A: No. I know that feeling, mate. When I got signed off, the first year, I felt like I'd lost a bit of myself, you know. You think you're no use. But you're not, it's just a gap. You'll be back on a shift before you know it.
B: Yeah. Hope so.
A: You will. Do the CV tonight, get it done. Put the deliveries at the top, and the stock.
B: That's what he said.
A: Well then, two of us can't be wrong, can we? And you tell Jess I said—
